F1.quote: A public interest and scholarly project to document protests and demonstrations in the United States.
F1.claim: the consortium's own definition: a public interest and scholarly project documenting protests and demonstrations in the United States
F1.lineage: what it is: a public interest and scholarly project documenting protest in the United States

F2.quote: The Crowd Counting Consortium (CCC) is a joint project of Harvard Kennedy School and the University of Connecticut that collects publicly available data on political protest events reported in the United States, including rallies, marches, demonstrations, and acts of civil disobedience.
F2.claim: a joint project of HKS and UConn collecting publicly available data on political protest events reported in the US: rallies, marches, demonstrations, acts of civil disobedience
F2.lineage: what it is: a public interest and scholarly project documenting protest in the United States

F3.claim: part of the Nonviolent Action Lab
F3.lineage: operator and institutional home: Harvard Kennedy School, UConn, the Nonviolent Action Lab

F4.quote: The CCC first emerged from a collaborative effort by Jeremy Pressman (UConn) and Erica Chenoweth (HKS) to estimate the number of participants in the Women’s March on Washington (and its affiliated sister marches nationwide) on January 21, 2017.
F4.claim: it emerged from Pressman and Chenoweth’s effort to estimate the participants in the Women’s March of 21 January 2017
F4.lineage: origin and founders: the Women’s March of 21 January 2017

F5.quote: Since then, the project has expanded to provide near-real-time information on trends in the occurrence, themes, and scale of American protest activity.
F5.claim: it has expanded to near-real-time information on the occurrence, themes and scale of American protest
F5.lineage: what it is: a public interest and scholarly project documenting protest in the United States

F6.quote: CCC data are published monthly on a publicly accessible Dataverse, for use by scholars, journalists, movement leaders, and others.
F6.claim: the data are published monthly on a public Dataverse for scholars, journalists, movement leaders and others
F6.lineage: data access: the Dataverse, monthly; Google Sheets; a weekly compilation

F7.quote: The NVA Lab regularly publishes commentary and analysis pieces based on the CCC data, advancing both scholarly and public understandings of protest in the US.
F7.claim: the Nonviolent Action Lab publishes commentary and analysis on the data

F8.quote: CCC data were used to demonstrate that, at that time, the 2017 Women’s March was the largest single-day demonstration in US history.
F8.claim: its data showed the 2017 Women’s March the largest single-day demonstration in US history at that time
F8.lineage: uses: the record against prevailing narratives

F9.quote: CCC data were used to demonstrate that, at that time, the 2018 March for Our Lives and #Enough Walkouts were the broadest single day demonstration if U.S. history (occurring in over 4400 distinct locations).
F9.claim: its data showed the 2018 March for Our Lives and #Enough Walkouts the broadest single-day demonstration at that time, in over 4,400 locations
F9.lineage: uses: the record against prevailing narratives

F10.quote: CCC data underlie an influential New York Times analysis demonstrating that, at that time, protests in 2020 following George Floyd’s murder constituted the largest and broadest mobilization in U.S. history.
F10.claim: its data underlie a New York Times analysis of the 2020 protests after George Floyd’s murder as the largest and broadest mobilization at that time
F10.lineage: uses: the record against prevailing narratives

F11.quote: Relatedly, CCC data support the claim that the 2020 Black Lives Matter uprising was overwhelmingly peaceful , especially relative to the heavy-handed police response.
F11.claim: its data support the claim that the 2020 Black Lives Matter uprising was overwhelmingly peaceful
F11.lineage: uses: the record against prevailing narratives

F12.quote: CCC data underpin an analysis of the 2023-2024 pro-Palestine protests, which were also generally peaceful , despite common narratives that the protests were violent.
F12.claim: its data underpin an analysis of the 2023–2024 pro-Palestine protests as generally peaceful, against narratives of violence
F12.lineage: uses: the record against prevailing narratives

F13.quote: Most recently, the CCC data have been used to rebut the narrative that there is “no resistance” to the second Trump administration. Instead, the CCC data demonstrate higher degrees of protest throughout 2025 than in 2017, a high degree of nonviolent discipline among anti-Trump protesters, and an increasing number of protests (and protest participants) in counties where Trump won majorities in 2024.
F13.claim: its data rebut the narrative of “no resistance” to the second Trump administration: more protest in 2025 than in 2017, nonviolent discipline, growth in counties Trump won
F13.lineage: uses: the record against prevailing narratives

F14.quote: The CCC data also demonstrated that the No Kings protests in June and October of 2025 were among the largest single-day demonstrations in US history.
F14.claim: its data showed the No Kings protests of June and October 2025 among the largest single-day demonstrations in US history
F14.lineage: uses: the record against prevailing narratives

F15.quote: Academics routinely turn to the CCC data to study protest, counter-protest, and state response. Articles and essays published by the CCC team since 2017 have collectively garnered more than 600 scholarly citations so far.
F15.claim: academics use the data to study protest, counter-protest and state response; the team’s articles have more than 600 scholarly citations

F16.locus: Meet the Team; commentary of May 10, 2024
F16.quote: Erica Chenoweth … Frank Stanton Professor of the First Amendment … Jeremy Pressman … Senior Research Fellow, AY2025-2027 … Christopher Shay … Research Associate, Crowd Counting Consortium … Nonviolent Action Lab Program Director Jay Ulfelder
F16.claim: the team: Erica Chenoweth, Jeremy Pressman, a research associate of the consortium among others; Jay Ulfelder the Lab’s program director
F16.lineage: operator and institutional home: Harvard Kennedy School, UConn, the Nonviolent Action Lab

F17.quote: Protest event data from CCC’s three phases — 2017-2020, 2021-2024, and 2025 to the present — can be downloaded from the project’s Dataverse.
F17.claim: the data in three phases, 2017–2020, 2021–2024, 2025 to the present, downloadable from the Dataverse
F17.lineage: data access: the Dataverse, monthly; Google Sheets; a weekly compilation

F18.quote: We only post records that we can confirm and verify through fact-checking. When you submit a record, be sure to provide a source that is publicly verifiable
F18.claim: only records confirmed and verified by fact-checking are posted; a submission must carry a publicly verifiable source
F18.lineage: verification and privacy: the rules that bound the record

F19.quote: We will never post, release, or share identifying information that has not already been reported in the public domain.
F19.claim: it will never share identifying information not already reported in the public domain
F19.lineage: verification and privacy: the rules that bound the record

F20.locus: FAQ, What kind of actions are you collecting?
F20.quote: We collect publicly available data on political crowds reported in the United States, including marches, protests, demonstrations, riots, and other actions. We do not count crowds at meetings, teach-ins or academic workshops, panel discussions, fundraisers, or town halls.
F20.claim: its unit: political crowds reported in the US, riots among them; crowds at meetings, teach-ins, workshops, panels, fundraisers and town halls excluded
F20.lineage: the unit: what counts as a political crowd

F21.locus: FAQ, What do you intend to do with these data?
F21.quote: Our goal is to make the aggregate data on crowd numbers publicly available for each event. We are collecting this data in the public interest and to further scholarly research.
F21.claim: its goal: aggregate crowd numbers public for each event, in the public interest and for research
F21.lineage: what it is: a public interest and scholarly project documenting protest in the United States

F22.quote: This is a public-interest project. The University of Denver’s Office of Research Integrity and Education determined that the project does not qualify as human subjects research and therefore does not require further review or oversight by its Institutional Review Board. The University of Connecticut made a similar determination.
F22.claim: the University of Denver and UConn determined that it is not human subjects research
F22.lineage: verification and privacy: the rules that bound the record

F23.locus: FAQ, Where can I get the data?; How should I cite these data?
F23.quote: The data and associated documentation are shared via the Harvard Dataverse … Please include a citation to the Crowd Counting Consortium such as: Crowd Counting Consortium, crowdcounting.org, accessed September 17, 2021.
F23.claim: data and documentation on the Harvard Dataverse; the citation form names crowdcounting.org
F23.lineage: data access: the Dataverse, monthly; Google Sheets; a weekly compilation

F24.locus: FAQ, Where does your funding come from?
F24.quote: Funding is made possible in part by the Freedom Together Foundation, New Venture Fund, Humanity United, the John T. and Catherine D. MacArthur Foundation … Previously, we received support from the Carnegie Corporation of New York
F24.claim: funded in part by foundations and university centres, previously by the Carnegie Corporation of New York

F25.quote: We have collaborated with countlove.org , a volunteer group that developed a webcrawler to identify protests and demonstrations on a daily basis.
F25.claim: it has collaborated with countlove.org, a volunteer group whose webcrawler identifies protests daily
F25.lineage: method: public reports, verified submissions, a webcrawler

F26.quote: From 7 October 2023 to 7 June 2024, the Crowd Counting Consortium recorded nearly 12,400 pro-Palestine protests and over 2,000 pro-Israel protests in the United States. … Oct 23, 2024
F26.claim: nearly 12,400 pro-Palestine and over 2,000 pro-Israel protests recorded, 7 October 2023 to 7 June 2024

F27.quote: Crowd Counting Consortium data show more than 3,700 days with pro-Palestinian protest activity at over 500 U.S. schools since October 7, 2023, including encampments at more than 130 of them.
F27.claim: pro-Palestinian protest at over 500 US schools since 7 October 2023, encampments at more than 130

F28.quote: New data shows No Kings was one of the largest days of protest in US history … Aug 15, 2025
F28.claim: the latest commentary listed on the page, 15 August 2025

F29.quote: Blog of the Crowd Counting Consortium
F29.claim: Counting Crowds is the consortium’s blog

F30.quote: CCC records and shares its data in monthly Google Sheets, which you can find on the project’s View/Download the Data page .
F30.claim: the data shared in monthly Google Sheets
F30.lineage: data access: the Dataverse, monthly; Google Sheets; a weekly compilation

F31.quote: A compiled and augmented version of the complete dataset can be found in this GitHub repository , which is maintained by the Harvard Kennedy School’s Nonviolent Action Lab . We update that compiled version weekly, usually on Wednesdays.
F31.claim: a compiled and augmented version kept on GitHub by the Nonviolent Action Lab, updated weekly, usually on Wednesdays
F31.lineage: data access: the Dataverse, monthly; Google Sheets; a weekly compilation

F32.quote: You can also explore the compiled data online using this interactive dashboard .
F32.claim: an interactive dashboard of the compiled data
F32.lineage: data access: the Dataverse, monthly; Google Sheets; a weekly compilation

F33.quote: The Crowd Counting Consortium (CCC) is a collaborative project between Harvard University and University of Connecticut that has systematically collected data on political protest events across the United States since January 2017. The dataset encompasses rallies, marches, demonstrations, and acts of civil disobedience that articulate grievances against or express support for political targets.
F33.claim: a third party restates the consortium: a Harvard–UConn project collecting data on US political protest events since January 2017, events that articulate grievances against or support for political targets
F33.lineage: what it is: a public interest and scholarly project documenting protest in the United States

F34.quote: The dataset includes events that are open to the public, free of charge, and nonviolent (not primarily organized to cause direct harm to persons). Coverage extends to all U.S. states and territories, with no minimum crowd size requirement.
F34.claim: the third party gives the dataset’s events as public, free and nonviolent (not primarily organized to cause direct harm), in all US states and territories, with no minimum crowd size
F34.lineage: the unit: what counts as a political crowd

F35.quote: Virtual gatherings are included alongside physical events, reflecting the evolution of collective action especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. Excluded are activities like paid fundraisers, workshops, campaign events closed to the public, and routine government meetings unless deliberately disrupted by protesters.
F35.claim: virtual gatherings included; paid fundraisers, workshops, closed campaign events and routine government meetings excluded unless disrupted
F35.lineage: the unit: what counts as a political crowd
